case_studies.title: LLMs Improving LLMs: Agentic Discovery for Test-Time Scaling
case_studies.abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) has become an effective approach for improving large language model performance by allocating additional computation during inference. However, existing TTS strategies are largely hand-crafted: researchers manually design reasoning patterns and tune heuristics by intuition, leaving much of the computation-allocation space unexplored. We propose an environment-driven framework, AutoTTS, that changes what researchers design: from individual TTS heuristics to environments where TTS strategies can be discovered automatically. The key to AutoTTS lies in environment construct
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of inefficient large language model performance by introducing an automated framework called AutoTTS, which discovers optimal test-time scaling strategies, resulting in improved model performance. The authors built an environment-driven framework that automatically allocates computation during inference. This research may impact IT infrastructure work related to large language models and AI applications.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage large language model infrastructure, here is what to do: review your current test-time scaling strategies, consider implementing AutoTTS to automate computation allocation, and monitor performance improvements. This flags a risk: if your org relies on manual TTS strategies, check for potential inefficiencies and explore automated alternatives like AutoTTS. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work outside of AI and large language models.

case_studies.title: Coding Agents Don't Know When to Act
case_studies.abstract: Coding agents are increasingly deployed to autonomously maintain software, including to resolve user-reported issues: a bug report comes in and the agent creates a patch to address it. However, in any real-world deployment, they will encounter stale bug reports about issues that have already been resolved. Agents should recognize this and abstain from modifying the code to avoid accumulating technical debt. To systematically evaluate whether current agents do so, we introduce FixedBench, a code benchmark with 200 human-verified coding tasks in which no code changes are required, testing five r
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of coding agents unnecessarily modifying code for already resolved issues, by introducing FixedBench, a code benchmark to evaluate agents' ability to recognize stale bug reports, resulting in improved agent performance. The researchers built FixedBench with 200 human-verified coding tasks to test agents' decision-making. This research aims to reduce technical debt accumulation in software maintenance.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage autonomous coding agents for software maintenance, here is what to do: assess your agents' ability to recognize stale bug reports, evaluate their performance using a benchmark like FixedBench, and adjust their decision-making logic to avoid unnecessary code changes.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty: Academic novelty (2) plus potential novelty for IT agents who use coding agents (3). IT Relevance: Directly relevant to how IT engineers work with coding agents (16). Value 90 Days: Potential to flag a risk and propose a service for clients (8). Low_signal: false.

case_studies.title: Abductive Reasoning with Probabilistic Commonsense
case_studies.abstract: Recent efforts to improve the reasoning abilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) have focused on integrating formal logic solvers within neurosymbolic frameworks. A key challenge is that formal solvers lack commonsense world knowledge, preventing them from making reasoning steps that humans find obvious. Prior methods address this by using LLMs to supply missing commonsense assumptions, but these approaches implicitly assume universal agreement on such commonsense facts. In reality, commonsense beliefs vary across individuals. We propose a probabilistic framework for abductive commonsense rea
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of limited commonsense knowledge in formal logic solvers used in Large Language Models. The researchers built a probabilistic framework for abductive reasoning that incorporates varying commonsense beliefs. The result is a more human-like reasoning ability in Large Language Models.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses a key challenge in integrating formal and symbolic reasoning into LLMs. The probabilistic framework for abductive commonsense reasoning reveals something potentially interesting to IT engineers working with ML models.

case_studies.title: Self-Play Enhancement via Advantage-Weighted Refinement in Online Federated LLM Fine-Tuning with Real-Time Feedback
case_studies.abstract: Recent works have advanced feedback-based learning systems, whereby a foundation model is able to intake incoming feedback (e.g., a user) to self-improve, creating a self-loop system of training. However, existing works are limited in needing to consider an offline setup to allow for such feedback-based methods, and are further limited in the need of requiring privileged ground-truth contexts for training. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of limited feedback-based learning systems by building a self-play enhancement model that refines online federated large language model fine-tuning with real-time feedback. The result is a more efficient and effective way to incorporate external feedback across large networks of end users. This does not directly affect cloud infrastructure management work.

case_studies.title: Switchcraft: AI Model Router for Agentic Tool Calling
case_studies.abstract: Agentic AI systems that invoke external tools are powerful but costly, leading developers to default to large models and overspend inference budgets. Model routing can mitigate this, but existing routers are designed for chat completion rather than tool use. We present Switchcraft, the first (to the best of our knowledge) model router optimized for agentic tool calling. Switchcraft operates inline, selecting the lowest-cost model subject to correctness. We construct an evaluation framework on five function-calling benchmarks and train a DistilBERT-based classifier, deployed under a latency bud
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of overspending on large AI models by developing Switchcraft, a model router that optimizes the selection of AI models for tool calling. Switchcraft operates in real-time, choosing the lowest-cost model that meets the required standards. The result is a more efficient use of resources without compromising performance.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI infrastructure, consider implementing a model router like Switchcraft to optimize your model selection and reduce costs: step 1, assess your current model usage and costs, step 2, evaluate the suitability of Switchcraft or similar routers for your use case, step 3, deploy and monitor the router's performance to ensure it meets your requirements.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelity: The idea of a model router for agentic tool calling is new and potentially impactful. IT Relevance: While relevant to AI infrastructure, the specific focus on agentic tool calling may not be directly relevant to every IT engineer. Value: While theoretically useful, the practical impact and feasibility of implementing this within 90 days is low.

case_studies.title: Rubric-Grounded RL: Structured Judge Rewards for Generalizable Reasoning
case_studies.abstract: We argue that decomposing reward into weighted, verifiable criteria and using an LLM judge to score them provides a partial-credit optimization signal: instead of a binary outcome or a single holistic score, each response is graded along multiple task-specific criteria. We formalize \emph{rubric-grounded reinforcement learning (RL)}: a framework in which the policy is optimized against a structured, multi-criterion reward produced by a frozen LLM judge that conditions on auxiliary grounding the policy never sees. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of limited reward signals in reinforcement learning by creating a framework that decomposes rewards into weighted, verifiable criteria. The authors built a rubric-grounded reinforcement learning framework that uses a large language model to score responses based on multiple task-specific criteria. The result is a more generalizable and robust optimization signal.

case_studies.title: The Memory Curse: How Expanded Recall Erodes Cooperative Intent in LLM Agents
case_studies.abstract: Context window expansion is often treated as a straightforward capability upgrade for LLMs, but we find it systematically fails in multi-agent social dilemmas. Across 7 LLMs and 4 games over 500 rounds, expanding accessible history degrades cooperation in 18 of 28 model--game settings, a pattern we term the memory curse. We isolate the underlying mechanism through three analyses. First, lexical analysis of 378,000 reasoning traces associates this breakdown with eroding forward-looking intent rather than rising paranoia. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of how expanded recall affects cooperative intent in large language models, finding that it can actually degrade cooperation, which they term the 'memory curse'. They built and tested 7 language models in 4 games over 500 rounds. The result shows that expanding accessible history can lead to less cooperation in many model-game settings.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on the behavior of large language models in social dilemmas rather than cloud infrastructure management.

case_studies.title: Dooly: Configuration-Agnostic, Redundancy-Aware Profiling for LLM Inference Simulation
case_studies.abstract: Selecting the optimal LLM inference configuration requires evaluation across hardware, serving engines, attention backends, and model architectures, since no single choice performs best across all workloads. Profile-based simulators are the standard tool, yet they hardcode their operation set to a specific configuration and re-profile every operation from scratch, making exploration prohibitively expensive. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of optimising Large Language Model (LLM) inference configuration by building a configuration-agnostic profiling tool called Dooly, which reduces the cost of exploring different configurations. The result is a more efficient way to evaluate LLM inference configurations across different hardware and software setups. This research focuses on LLM inference and does not directly impact general cloud infrastructure management.
